content: A chalazion is a small, localized swelling on the eyelid that occurs due to a blockage in one of the tiny oil-producing glands, known as Meibomian glands. These glands are responsible for secreting the oil that helps lubricate the surface of the eye. Each eyelid contains approximately 100 of these glands, located near the base of the eyelashes. When the duct of one of these glands becomes obstructed, it can lead to the formation of a chalazion. The symptoms of a chalazion include tenderness of the eyelid, increased tearing, painful swelling on the eyelid, and sensitivity to light. These symptoms can vary in severity depending on the size and location of the chalazion. To diagnose a chalazion, a healthcare provider will perform a physical examination of the eyelid. In rare cases, a blocked Meibomian gland duct may be caused by a skin cancer. If this is suspected, a biopsy may be necessary to confirm the diagnosis. If the swelling worsens or persists for more than one month despite treatment, it is important to contact a healthcare provider. Additionally, if the lump on the eyelid continues to grow or is associated with loss of eyelashes, a medical evaluation is recommended. Warm compresses should be applied to the affected eyelid for 10-15 minutes at least four times a day. This helps to soften the hardened oils that are blocking the duct, promoting drainage and healing. In many cases, a chalazion will resolve on its own within a month without further intervention. However, if the chalazion continues to enlarge or does not improve, surgical removal may be necessary. This procedure is typically performed from the underside of the eyelid to avoid leaving a visible scar. Antibiotic eye drops are often prescribed for use before and after the surgical procedure, but they are not generally effective in treating a chalazion on their own. Another treatment option is a steroid injection, which may help reduce inflammation. The prognosis for a chalazion is generally excellent. Most chalazia resolve on their own or respond well to treatment. This complication typically resolves once the chalazion is treated. To prevent the recurrence of chalazia, individuals who are prone to this condition should practice proper eyelid hygiene. Cleaning the eyelid area with a gentle cleanser, such as baby shampoo, can help reduce the risk of duct blockages and prevent the formation of new chalazia.
